## Why This Matters

L03 ended on a deliberate anticlimax: the million-row table you benchmarked is **not** big data --
it crunches in milliseconds on one machine. So what genuinely requires more? The answer shaped a
whole industry: when one machine is not enough, you **split the work, compute locally, and assemble
the answer** -- and you should know both how that works and when it is overkill. L03 told you scaling
out *exists*; this lesson shows the *mechanics*.

::: {.callout-tip title="Analogy: the census, formalized"}
A census of Puerto Rico. One option: a single, very fast clerk reads every form on the island (scale
**up**). The other: each of the 78 municipalities counts its own forms locally (**map**), mails one
subtotal per question to the capital (**shuffle**), where the subtotals are added up (**reduce**)
(scale **out**). MapReduce is the 78-clerks idea, formalized -- and Spark is the modern machine that
runs it.
:::

## Splitting the Work: HDFS and MapReduce

The storage half is a **distributed file system** (Hadoop's is HDFS): one huge file is chopped into
blocks, the blocks are spread across many machines, and each block is stored on more than one machine
(machines fail; the data must survive). That raises the question: how do you compute on a file that
lives in pieces on fifty machines?

**MapReduce** answers with a discipline of three phases:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    F[Input, split in chunks] --> M1[Map worker 1]
    F --> M2[Map worker 2]
    F --> M3[Map worker 3]
    M1 --> S[Shuffle: route pairs by key]
    M2 --> S
    M3 --> S
    S --> R1[Reduce: key group A]
    S --> R2[Reduce: key group B]
    R1 --> O[Assembled answer]
    R2 --> O
```

Reading the diagram: **map** runs on each chunk *where it is stored* -- no data movement, full
parallelism -- turning records into `(key, value)` pairs. **Shuffle** is the only phase that moves
data: every pair travels to the worker responsible for its key. **Reduce** collapses each key's
bucket into a result, again in parallel. The pandas `groupby` you have used since L02 secretly has
this shape -- map (emit the group key), shuffle (gather each group), reduce (aggregate) -- which is
why the lab can write MapReduce in a dozen-odd lines of plain Python before touching any framework.

## Spark: MapReduce, Industrialized

Writing raw map and reduce jobs by hand (Hadoop's original programming model) proved verbose and
slow -- every intermediate result was written to disk. **Apache Spark** kept the paradigm and fixed
the ergonomics:

| | Hadoop MapReduce | Spark |
|---|------------------|-------|
| You write | map and reduce functions, by hand | DataFrame operations (`groupBy`, `agg`) -- the `groupby` shape from L02 |
| Intermediate data | written to disk between phases | kept in **memory** across steps |
| Execution | eager, one job at a time | **lazy**: builds a plan, optimizes it, runs on demand |
| Today | legacy (its filesystem, HDFS, lives on) | the de facto standard for cluster compute |

Two Spark words you will meet in the lab. The **driver** is your notebook process -- it holds the
plan; **executors** are the workers that hold data partitions and do the computing. In **local mode**
(what the lab uses), driver and executors all run on your one machine, using every core -- a
one-machine rehearsal of a cluster.

And **lazy evaluation**: `groupBy(...).agg(...)` returns instantly because *nothing has run* -- Spark
just recorded the plan. Only an **action** (`.show()`, `.count()`, a write) triggers execution, which
lets Spark optimize the whole pipeline first. In the lab you will read one of those plans with
`.explain()` and watch it pull L03's trick: reading only the two columns the query needs from the
Parquet file.

## When NOT to Use a Cluster

- **Stay on the laptop when:** the data fits on one machine (rule of thumb: up to tens of GB with
  pandas or a single-machine database), the job runs comfortably overnight, or you are iterating on a
  sample anyway. Spark's startup and shuffle overhead make it *slower* than pandas at laptop scale --
  clusters buy *capacity*, not free speed.
- **Scale out when:** the data genuinely exceeds one machine's disk or RAM, a pipeline must finish
  faster than one machine allows, or the data already lives in a distributed store and moving it out
  costs more than computing in place.
- The professional default order of escalation: **sample it, then laptop, then one big machine, then
  cluster** -- and most projects never reach the last step.

## FAQ / Industry Reality

**"Is Hadoop dead, then?"** -- The *programming model* (hand-written MapReduce jobs) is legacy; the
*ideas* won completely. HDFS-style distributed storage underlies modern data lakes, and Spark, which
replaced it at the compute layer, is itself a MapReduce descendant -- today usually rented as a
managed service (Databricks, AWS EMR, Google Dataproc) rather than self-hosted. Learn the paradigm,
not the brand.

**"My 50 GB CSV -- is that big data?"** -- Almost certainly not. Convert it to Parquet (L03), point a
single-machine engine at it, and it is an interactive dataset on one machine. *"Does not fit in
Excel"* is not the bar; *"does not fit on a machine"* is.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Optional deep dive: RDDs vs DataFrames"}
Spark's original API, the **RDD** (Resilient Distributed Dataset), exposes map and reduce directly
over arbitrary Python objects -- maximum control, no optimizer help. The **DataFrame** API you use in
the lab describes *what* you want in named-column operations, letting Spark's optimizer reorder,
prune, and fuse the work (the `.explain()` plan is its output). The relationship mirrors L02: an RDD
is the imperative loop, a DataFrame the declarative query. Modern Spark code is DataFrames almost
exclusively; RDDs surface only when structure truly disappears.
:::
